subtopic: Symptomatic bradycardia: IV atropine first
stem: A 74-year-old man is brought to an emergency department in Ballina, NSW, after feeling faint all morning. He is pale and sweaty. Pulse 36/min and regular, BP 82/50 mmHg. His ECG shows sinus bradycardia at 36/min with a normal QRS. He takes no rate-slowing medicines and has not had a cardiac transplant.
lead_in: Which one of the following is the most appropriate initial drug treatment?

options.A: Intravenous adrenaline infusion as the first drug
options.C: Intravenous amiodarone 300 mg
options.D: Observation only because sinus rhythm is present
options.E: Intravenous atropine 500–600 micrograms, repeated every 3–5 minutes as needed

explanation_correct: He has a bradyarrhythmia with adverse signs (systolic BP <90 mmHg, heart rate <40/min). ANZCOR Guideline 11.9 says atropine is the first treatment: 500–600 micrograms IV, repeated every 3–5 minutes up to 3 mg. If this fails, low-dose adrenaline is the second-line drug, with pacing for patients who do not respond or who are at high risk of asystole.

option_explanations.A: ANZCOR lists adrenaline as second-line, after atropine fails.
option_explanations.B: Adenosine is for regular narrow-complex tachycardia, not bradycardia.
option_explanations.C: Amiodarone is an antiarrhythmic for tachyarrhythmias and would worsen bradycardia.
option_explanations.D: Bradycardia with hypotension and heart rate <40/min needs immediate treatment.

key_learning_point: Bradycardia with adverse signs: give IV atropine 500–600 mcg (up to 3 mg), then adrenaline or pacing if that fails.

subtopic: Regular narrow-complex tachycardia: adenosine unmasks atrial flutter
stem: A 66-year-old woman presents to an emergency department in Warrnambool, Vic, with palpitations for three hours. She is alert, BP 128/78 mmHg. ECG shows a regular narrow-complex tachycardia at 150/min. A modified Valsalva manoeuvre has no effect. During IV adenosine 6 mg, the rhythm strip shows the ventricular rate slow briefly, revealing regular saw-tooth atrial activity at about 300/min, before the tachycardia at 150/min returns.
lead_in: Which one of the following is the most likely rhythm?

options.A: Atrial flutter with 2:1 atrioventricular conduction
options.C: AV re-entry tachycardia via an accessory pathway

explanation_correct: ANZCOR Guideline 11.9 notes that if the ventricular rate slows briefly with adenosine but the arrhythmia continues, you should look for atrial flutter or another atrial tachycardia. Saw-tooth flutter waves at about 300/min with a ventricular rate of 150/min indicate atrial flutter with 2:1 conduction. Adenosine blocks the AV node but does not end a rhythm generated within the atria.

option_explanations.B: AVNRT depends on the AV node and usually terminates with adenosine rather than revealing flutter waves.
option_explanations.C: AVRT also uses the AV node and usually terminates with adenosine.
option_explanations.D: There are saw-tooth flutter waves rather than P waves, and the rate is fixed at 150/min.
option_explanations.E: The QRS is narrow.

key_learning_point: If adenosine only briefly slows a regular narrow-complex tachycardia and reveals saw-tooth waves, it is atrial flutter.

subtopic: Irregular broad-complex tachycardia in WPW: avoid AV nodal blockers
stem: A 24-year-old man with known Wolff–Parkinson–White pattern presents to an emergency department in Newcastle, NSW, with palpitations for one hour. He is alert, BP 112/70 mmHg. ECG shows an irregularly irregular broad-complex tachycardia at 210–250/min, with QRS complexes that vary in width from beat to beat.
lead_in: Which one of the following is the most appropriate interpretation and plan?

options.A: AF with bundle branch block; give IV verapamil for rate control
options.B: Monomorphic VT; give IV adenosine to clarify the rhythm
options.C: Pre-excited atrial fibrillation; avoid adenosine, digoxin, verapamil and diltiazem, and plan electrical cardioversion
options.D: AF with rapid ventricular response; give IV digoxin
options.E: Sinus tachycardia with aberrancy; give fluids

explanation_correct: An irregular broad-complex tachycardia with varying QRS width in a patient with WPW suggests atrial fibrillation conducting down the accessory pathway. ANZCOR Guideline 11.9 states that if pre-excited AF is suspected, adenosine, digoxin, verapamil and diltiazem should be avoided. These drugs block the AV node and cause a relative increase in pre-excitation, which can degenerate to VF. Electrical cardioversion is usually the safest treatment.

option_explanations.A: In WPW, AV nodal blockers can accelerate conduction down the accessory pathway.
option_explanations.B: The rhythm is irregular, and adenosine is contraindicated in pre-excited AF.
option_explanations.D: Digoxin is specifically listed to avoid in pre-excited AF.
option_explanations.E: The rhythm is irregularly irregular and at 250/min, so it is not sinus.

key_learning_point: Pre-excited AF (WPW with irregular broad complexes): avoid AV nodal blockers. Electrical cardioversion is usually safest.

subtopic: AF for more than 48 hours: TOE before early cardioversion
stem: A 59-year-old man in Bendigo, Vic, has had palpitations for about five days. ECG shows atrial fibrillation at 105/min. He is stable, with BP 134/82 mmHg. He is not taking an anticoagulant. The cardiology team would like to restore sinus rhythm during this admission rather than wait weeks.
lead_in: Which one of the following investigations is required before early cardioversion?

options.A: Transthoracic echocardiography
options.C: Transoesophageal echocardiography to exclude left atrial thrombus

explanation_correct: ANZCOR Guideline 11.9 states that patients who have been in AF for more than 48 hours should not have electrical or chemical cardioversion until they are fully anticoagulated, unless transoesophageal echocardiography has shown there is no atrial clot. Transthoracic echo cannot reliably exclude left atrial appendage thrombus.

option_explanations.A: TTE cannot reliably exclude left atrial appendage thrombus.
option_explanations.B: Troponin does not assess the risk of thromboembolism from cardioversion.
option_explanations.D: TFTs are useful for finding a cause, but they do not make cardioversion safe.
option_explanations.E: Holter monitoring is not needed. AF is already documented.

key_learning_point: AF for more than 48 hours: cardiovert only after full anticoagulation or after TOE excludes atrial clot.

subtopic: Hepatitis C cure: HCV RNA at least 12 weeks after treatment (SVR12)
stem: A 45-year-old woman in Launceston, Tas, has just finished 12 weeks of sofosbuvir/velpatasvir for chronic hepatitis C. She has no cirrhosis. She took every dose, and her ALT is now normal. She asks how she will know she is cured.
lead_in: Which one of the following tests best confirms cure?

options.A: HCV RNA by sensitive PCR at least 12 weeks after completing treatment
options.C: HCV RNA on the last day of treatment

explanation_correct: The Australian HCV guidelines define cure (sustained virological response, SVR12) as undetectable HCV RNA on a highly sensitive PCR assay at least 12 weeks after DAA therapy finishes. Late relapse after SVR is very uncommon. Anti-HCV antibodies are expected to stay positive and do not indicate active infection.

option_explanations.B: Antibodies stay positive after cure, so they cannot confirm it.
option_explanations.C: An end-of-treatment result does not rule out relapse. Cure is defined by the result at 12 weeks.
option_explanations.D: ALT is useful for follow-up but does not confirm viral cure.
option_explanations.E: Genotype does not assess response to treatment.

key_learning_point: Hepatitis C cure is SVR12: undetectable HCV RNA at least 12 weeks after DAA treatment ends.

subtopic: Positive HCV antibody after documented cure
stem: A 52-year-old man in Wollongong, NSW, was treated for hepatitis C three years ago. HCV RNA was undetectable 12 weeks after treatment, and he has no cirrhosis. A recent insurance medical showed a positive HCV antibody. He has not injected drugs since treatment. Today his HCV RNA is undetectable and his ALT is 24 U/L.
lead_in: Which one of the following is the most appropriate interpretation?

options.A: Relapse of hepatitis C requiring retreatment
options.C: Protective immunity against future HCV infection
options.D: Persistent antibody after cure; he does not have active infection and is not immune to reinfection
options.E: A false-positive antibody result that should be investigated with a liver biopsy

explanation_correct: The Australian HCV guidelines state that anti-HCV antibodies are expected to persist after SVR. They do not mean active infection, and they do not give immunity to reinfection. People without cirrhosis whose LFTs are normal after SVR do not need further specialist liver follow-up. Future testing for reinfection must use HCV RNA, not antibody.

option_explanations.A: His HCV RNA is undetectable.
option_explanations.B: Reinfection would show detectable HCV RNA.
option_explanations.C: Antibodies do not protect against reinfection.
option_explanations.E: The antibody is expected after past infection, and a biopsy is not indicated.

key_learning_point: After HCV cure, antibodies stay positive. Use HCV RNA to test for reinfection.

subtopic: Treated chlamydia: retest for reinfection at 3 months
stem: A 21-year-old woman in Townsville, Qld, was treated with doxycycline for 7 days for genital chlamydia found on screening. She is not pregnant, and her symptoms have gone. Her partner has also been treated. She asks whether she needs another test.
lead_in: Which one of the following is the most appropriate follow-up testing?

options.A: Test of cure NAAT one week after treatment
options.B: Repeat chlamydia NAAT at 3 months to detect reinfection
options.C: No further testing at any time

option_explanations.D: Serology is not used for diagnosis or follow-up.
option_explanations.E: Ultrasound is not indicated for uncomplicated infection.

subtopic: Vitamin B12 deficiency: anti-intrinsic factor antibodies for suspected autoimmune gastritis
stem:
A 58-year-old woman in Orange, NSW, has fatigue and tingling in her feet. She eats a mixed diet and takes no medicines. She has hypothyroidism and vitiligo.

Investigations:
- Haemoglobin 104 g/L, MCV 108 fL
- Serum B12 90 pmol/L (>150)
- Folate and iron studies normal
lead_in: Which one of the following investigations is most appropriate to establish the cause?

options.A: Schilling test
options.C: Coeliac serology as the only test

explanation_correct: With no dietary or drug cause and with other autoimmune disease, autoimmune gastritis (pernicious anaemia) is likely. Australian Prescriber recommends testing for anti-intrinsic factor antibodies when autoimmune gastritis is suspected. If these are negative, anti-parietal cell antibodies, gastrin and gastroscopy should be considered. The cause matters because B12 absorption is irreversibly impaired in pernicious anaemia, so oral B12 is unreliable and IM treatment is needed.

option_explanations.A: The Schilling test is no longer available.
option_explanations.B: A biopsy is not needed for B12 deficiency.
option_explanations.C: This could be considered, but the autoimmune history points to autoimmune gastritis first.
option_explanations.D: Homocysteine supports the diagnosis of deficiency but does not identify the cause.

key_learning_point: If B12 deficiency suggests autoimmune gastritis, test anti-intrinsic factor antibodies. Pernicious anaemia needs IM B12.

subtopic: Staging acute kidney injury by KDIGO criteria
stem: A 70-year-old man is admitted to a hospital in Gosford, NSW, with pneumonia and sepsis. His baseline creatinine from two months ago is 90 µmol/L. On day 2 his creatinine is 200 µmol/L. Urine output has averaged 0.4 mL/kg/h over the last 8 hours. He is not on dialysis.
lead_in: Which one of the following is the correct KDIGO stage of his acute kidney injury?

options.A: Stage 1
options.C: Stage 2
options.D: Not AKI because urine output is above 0.3 mL/kg/h
options.E: AKI cannot be staged without a 24-hour urine collection

explanation_correct: KDIGO stages AKI by the worse of the creatinine and urine output criteria. Stage 1 is creatinine 1.5–1.9 times baseline (or a rise of ≥26.5 µmol/L), or urine output <0.5 mL/kg/h for 6–12 hours. Stage 2 is creatinine 2.0–2.9 times baseline, or <0.5 mL/kg/h for ≥12 hours. Stage 3 is creatinine ≥3.0 times baseline (or ≥353.6 µmol/L), urine output <0.3 mL/kg/h for ≥24 hours or anuria for ≥12 hours, or starting kidney replacement therapy. A creatinine of 200/90 is 2.2 times baseline, which is stage 2. The urine output of 0.4 mL/kg/h for 8 hours would only meet stage 1.

option_explanations.A: The urine output criterion alone would be stage 1, but the creatinine rise of 2.2 times baseline makes it stage 2.
option_explanations.B: Creatinine is not ≥3 times baseline, he does not meet the stage 3 urine output criteria, and he is not on kidney replacement therapy.
option_explanations.D: Creatinine criteria alone define AKI.
option_explanations.E: Staging uses creatinine and hourly urine output.

key_learning_point: KDIGO AKI stage is set by the worse of creatinine (1.5–1.9×, 2.0–2.9×, ≥3×) and urine output.

references.name: KDIGO Clinical Practice Guideline for Acute Kidney Injury (2012)

subtopic: Persistent hepatitis B vaccine non-responder after a needlestick: HBIG within 72 hours
stem: A 34-year-old nurse in Brisbane, Qld, had a needlestick injury two hours ago from a patient known to be HBsAg-positive. She is documented as a persistent non-responder to hepatitis B vaccine: anti-HBs stayed <10 mIU/mL after a full course and three further doses, and she has tested negative for hepatitis B infection.
lead_in: Which one of the following is the most appropriate hepatitis B prophylaxis?

options.A: No prophylaxis because she has been vaccinated
options.B: A single booster dose of hepatitis B vaccine alone
options.C: Start tenofovir post-exposure prophylaxis
options.D: Hepatitis B immunoglobulin as soon as possible, within 72 hours
options.E: Wait for her anti-HBs result before deciding

explanation_correct: The Australian Immunisation Handbook says persistent non-responders are probably not protected and should be told they need hepatitis B immunoglobulin within 72 hours of any parenteral or mucosal exposure to hepatitis B virus. Its post-exposure prophylaxis table covers exposure to an HBsAg-positive source. HBV and HIV/HCV baseline testing and follow-up also apply.

option_explanations.A: A persistent non-responder is not protected.
option_explanations.B: A booster will not give immediate protection to a known non-responder.
option_explanations.C: Antivirals are not the recommended hepatitis B post-exposure prophylaxis.
option_explanations.E: Her non-response is already documented, and the 72-hour window must not be missed.

key_learning_point: Persistent HBV vaccine non-responders exposed to HBsAg need HBIG within 72 hours.

subtopic: Chronic digoxin toxicity with compromise: digoxin immune Fab
stem:
An 86-year-old woman in Bundaberg, Qld, is brought in with three days of nausea, confusion and yellow-tinged vision. She takes digoxin 125 micrograms daily for atrial fibrillation. Her furosemide dose was recently increased, and she has had diarrhoea. Pulse 38/min with intermittent junctional rhythm, BP 86/50 mmHg.

Investigations:
- Serum digoxin 3.4 nmol/L
- Potassium 5.9 mmol/L
- Creatinine 190 µmol/L (baseline 95)
lead_in: Which one of the following is the most appropriate specific treatment?

options.A: IV calcium gluconate for the hyperkalaemia
options.C: Activated charcoal 50 g
options.D: Digoxin immune Fab, 1 vial (40 mg) IV over 30 minutes
options.E: Stop digoxin and observe without other treatment

explanation_correct: This is chronic digoxin accumulation (worse kidney function, diuretics) with cardiovascular compromise (bradycardia and hypotension). Queensland Poisons Information Centre antidote guidance for chronic digoxin accumulation with compromise is digoxin immune Fab, 1 vial (40 mg) diluted in 100 mL saline over 30 minutes. Chronic accumulation is more common than acute overdose.

option_explanations.A: Calcium is not the specific treatment, and digoxin Fab treats the hyperkalaemia caused by digoxin.
option_explanations.B: Digoxin has a large volume of distribution and is not removed effectively by dialysis.
option_explanations.C: Charcoal is for recent acute ingestion, not chronic accumulation.
option_explanations.E: She has bradycardia with hypotension, which needs antidote treatment.

key_learning_point: Chronic digoxin toxicity with compromise: digoxin Fab, 1 vial (40 mg) IV over 30 minutes (Qld PIC).

subtopic: Infective COPD exacerbation: 5 days of amoxycillin or doxycycline
stem: A 72-year-old woman with COPD sees her GP in Port Macquarie, NSW, with four days of increased breathlessness and more sputum, which has changed from white to green. She is not febrile. subtopic: COPD exacerbation without infective features: consider pulmonary embolism
stem: A 68-year-old man with COPD is admitted to a hospital in Mildura, Vic, with five days of worsening breathlessness and new right-sided pleuritic chest pain. Sputum is unchanged and white, and he is afebrile. He had a total knee replacement four weeks ago. Pulse 112/min, SpO2 87% on room air. Chest X-ray shows hyperinflation only.

options.A: Sputum culture
options.C: CT pulmonary angiography
options.D: D-dimer alone to decide whether to image

explanation_correct: COPD-X cites a systematic review in which 16% of patients hospitalised with a COPD exacerbation who had CT pulmonary angiography were found to have a pulmonary embolism. option_explanations.E: A repeat X-ray delays diagnosis.

subtopic: Hepatitis B vaccine: no response after a booster dose
stem: A 29-year-old medical student in Adelaide, SA, completed a 3-dose hepatitis B vaccine course as a child. Pre-placement anti-HBs was <10 mIU/mL, so she had a single booster dose. Four weeks after the booster, anti-HBs is still <10 mIU/mL.
lead_in: Which one of the following is the most appropriate next step?

options.A: Declare her immune because she completed a childhood course
options.B: Repeat a full 3-dose course straight away without checking for infection
options.C: Give hepatitis B immunoglobulin now
options.D: Test for hepatitis B infection (HBsAg and anti-HBc); if negative, give 2 more doses 1 month apart and recheck anti-HBs at least 4 weeks later

explanation_correct: The Australian Immunisation Handbook advises that people who still have anti-HBs <10 mIU/mL after a booster should be tested for hepatitis B infection. If that is negative, they are recommended to have 2 more doses 1 month apart, with the booster counted as the first of the 3 repeat doses. Anti-HBs is rechecked at least 4 weeks after the last dose. Persistent non-responders need HBIG after any exposure.

option_explanations.A: A level <10 mIU/mL after a booster means she is not protected.
option_explanations.B: Chronic infection must be excluded first, and the booster counts as dose 1.
option_explanations.C: HBIG is for post-exposure prophylaxis, not routine non-response.
option_explanations.E: Waiting delays protection.

key_learning_point: No response after a hepatitis B booster: exclude infection, then give 2 more doses and recheck anti-HBs at 4 weeks or more.

subtopic: Tardive dyskinesia after antiemetic exposure in an older adult
stem: A 77-year-old woman in Lismore, NSW, has had prochlorperazine 5 mg three times daily for dizziness for the past 10 weeks. Her daughter has noticed repetitive lip-smacking, chewing movements and tongue protrusion over the last two weeks. Her gait and arm movements are otherwise normal.

subtopic: Planned splenectomy: complete vaccines at least 2 weeks before surgery
stem: A 41-year-old woman in Hobart, Tas, with immune thrombocytopenia that has not responded to treatment is booked for elective laparoscopic splenectomy in five weeks. She is up to date with her routine adult vaccines but has never had additional pneumococcal, meningococcal or Hib vaccines.

subtopic: Emergency splenectomy: vaccinate before discharge if follow-up is unlikely
stem: A 30-year-old man from a remote station in western Queensland had an emergency splenectomy in Townsville five days ago after a motorbike crash. He is recovering well and wants to go home tomorrow. He lives 900 km away, and the team thinks he is unlikely to return for review.

option_explanations.D: Vaccines are still recommended.

subtopic: High-grade blunt splenic injury managed non-operatively: repeat CT angiography at days 3–5
stem: A 36-year-old woman was a restrained driver in a crash near Toowoomba, Qld. CT on arrival showed an AAST grade IV splenic laceration without active extravasation. She has stayed haemodynamically stable and is being managed non-operatively in the high dependency unit. Today is day 3, and her haemoglobin is stable.

options.A: Repeat CT angiography of the abdomen
options.B: No imaging if she remains stable
options.C: Abdominal ultrasound only
options.E: Repeat CT only at 6 weeks before she returns to sport

explanation_correct: The Queensland adult blunt splenic injury guideline recommends that high-grade injuries (AAST grade IV–V) be managed in HDU or ICU with repeat CT angiography 3 to 5 days after injury. This looks for delayed vascular injury such as pseudoaneurysm, which may need embolisation. Grade III injuries are managed on a specialised ward, with repeat CTA considered according to clinical need.

option_explanations.C: Ultrasound cannot reliably detect a pseudoaneurysm.
option_explanations.D: Surgery is not indicated while non-operative management is succeeding.
option_explanations.E: Delayed vascular injury occurs earlier than this.

key_learning_point: Grade IV–V blunt splenic injury managed non-operatively: HDU or ICU care and repeat CTA at days 3–5.

subtopic: Raised PSA with PI-RADS 3 lesion and low PSA density: biopsy not routinely indicated
stem: A 63-year-old man in Toowong, Qld, had a PSA of 4.6 µg/L, confirmed on repeat testing. Multiparametric MRI shows a prostate volume of 70 mL with a single PI-RADS 3 lesion, giving a PSA density of 0.07 µg/L/mL. Digital rectal examination is unremarkable. He has no family history of prostate cancer.
lead_in: Which one of the following is the most appropriate interpretation?

options.A: Biopsy is required for any PI-RADS 3 lesion
options.C: A PSMA PET scan is needed
options.D: Discharge from all follow-up because the MRI is normal
options.E: PI-RADS 3 with PSA density below 0.15; biopsy is not routinely needed and PSA monitoring can continue

explanation_correct: The 2026 Australian early detection guideline recommends biopsy for PI-RADS 4–5 lesions, or for PI-RADS 3 lesions when PSA density is 0.15 or more. With PI-RADS 3 and a PSA density of 0.07, the risk of clinically significant cancer is low, so the guideline says biopsy may not be required, subject to clinical assessment. Ongoing monitoring is appropriate. The higher PSA is explained by his large gland.

option_explanations.B: Cancer has not been diagnosed.
option_explanations.C: PSMA PET is a staging test, not a test to decide on biopsy.
option_explanations.D: The MRI is not normal, and ongoing PSA surveillance is still needed.

key_learning_point: PI-RADS 3 lesion: biopsy if PSA density is ≥0.15. Below that, monitor.

subtopic: Higher-risk man: PSA testing every 2 years from age 45
stem: A 45-year-old man sees his GP in Darwin, NT. His father was diagnosed with prostate cancer at 58. He has no urinary symptoms. After discussing the benefits and harms of testing, he decides he wants to be tested.

subtopic: Acute pancreatitis severity: CRP at 48 hours, not lipase level
stem: A 55-year-old woman is admitted to a hospital in Wagga Wagga, NSW, with gallstone pancreatitis. On admission her lipase was 4,800 U/L (<60). At 48 hours her lipase has fallen to 900 U/L and her CRP is 240 mg/L. A registrar suggests she is improving because her lipase has fallen.
lead_in: Which one of the following is the most accurate interpretation?

options.A: The CRP above 150 mg/L at 48 hours suggests severe pancreatitis; falling lipase does not indicate improvement
options.B: Falling lipase shows the pancreatitis is resolving
options.C: The very high initial lipase predicted severe disease
options.D: Repeat lipase daily to guide discharge

explanation_correct: Australian Prescriber notes that neither amylase nor lipase helps monitor or predict the severity of pancreatitis in adults, and the size of the rise does not predict severity. Daily measurements should not be used to judge disease activity. A CRP above 150 mg/L at 48 hours after symptom onset is the best single laboratory predictor of severity, alongside composite scores.

option_explanations.B: Lipase trends do not reflect severity or resolution.
option_explanations.C: The magnitude of the rise does not predict severity in adults.
option_explanations.D: Daily enzyme measurements are not recommended.
option_explanations.E: CRP at 48 hours is the best single laboratory predictor.

key_learning_point: In adult pancreatitis, a CRP above 150 mg/L at 48 hours predicts severity. Lipase levels do not.

subtopic: Life-threatening limb bleeding not controlled by pressure: arterial tourniquet
stem: A 38-year-old farm worker in Gympie, Qld, has a deep laceration to his right thigh from a chainsaw. Bright red blood is spurting from the wound despite firm direct pressure with a pad from a colleague. He is pale and sweaty, with a pulse of 130/min. An ambulance has been called, and a commercial windlass tourniquet is in the first aid kit. The colleague is trained in its use.
lead_in: Which one of the following is the most appropriate immediate action?

options.A: Elevate the leg and continue the same pressure
options.C: Prioritise airway positioning before bleeding control
options.D: Apply an arterial tourniquet above the wound, tighten until bleeding stops, and note the time
options.E: Remove the pad to inspect the wound every few minutes

explanation_correct: ANZCOR Guideline 9.1.1 states that firm direct pressure is the most effective way to stop most bleeding. Where life-threatening limb bleeding is not controlled by direct pressure, an arterial tourniquet is suggested if one is available and the first aider is trained in its use. It is applied above the bleeding point (5 cm above if there are no manufacturer instructions), not over a joint, and tightened until the bleeding stops. The time is recorded and passed on, and the tourniquet is not removed until the person reaches specialist care.

option_explanations.A: ANZCOR notes there is no evidence that elevation helps, and pressure has already failed.
option_explanations.B: Venous tourniquets are not suitable as arterial tourniquets.
option_explanations.C: In life-threatening bleeding, controlling the bleeding comes before airway and breathing interventions.
option_explanations.E: Repeatedly removing the pad lets the wound keep bleeding.

key_learning_point: If life-threatening limb bleeding continues despite pressure, apply an arterial tourniquet above the wound and record the time.

subtopic: Thermal burn first aid: at least 20 minutes of cool running water
stem: A 26-year-old chef in Fremantle, WA, spilt boiling water over his left forearm 40 minutes ago. He ran it under the tap for about two minutes and then wrapped it in a towel. He now attends the emergency department with a painful, blistered, red area about the size of his palm.

subtopic: Peritonitis with suspected perforation: CT as the first imaging test
stem: A 61-year-old man in Rockhampton, Qld, has had sudden severe upper abdominal pain for four hours. He takes naproxen for back pain. He has a rigid abdomen with generalised guarding. Pulse 108/min, BP 112/70 mmHg. An erect chest X-ray done in the department shows no free gas under the diaphragm.
lead_in: Which one of the following is the most appropriate next investigation?

options.A: Reassure: perforation is excluded by the chest X-ray
options.C: Left lateral decubitus X-ray first, then decide

explanation_correct: The WSES perforated peptic ulcer guideline notes that a negative X-ray does not rule out perforation. When there are clear signs of peritonitis, abdominal CT should be the first imaging test. CT shows free extraluminal gas and fluid and can help locate the perforation, so a normal erect X-ray should not delay CT and surgical review.

option_explanations.C: This gives similar accuracy to an erect film. CT is preferred when there is peritonitis.

option_explanations.E: Ultrasound is less sensitive for free gas.

key_learning_point: Suspected perforation with peritonitis: go to CT. A normal erect chest X-ray does not exclude it.

subtopic: Pertussis vaccine in each pregnancy at 20–32 weeks
stem: A 31-year-old woman in her second pregnancy attends her GP in Toowoomba, Qld, at 21 weeks' gestation. She had a dTpa vaccine during her first pregnancy two years ago and asks whether she needs another.

stem: A 2-year-old boy is brought to an emergency department in Bendigo, Vic, with 24 hours of diarrhoea and vomiting. subtopic: Minor head injury in a child: observation versus immediate CT
stem: A 5-year-old boy falls from a 1-metre playground platform in Wollongong, NSW, and bumps his forehead. His father saw a brief loss of consciousness lasting a few seconds before he cried. He has not vomited and has no headache. He now has a GCS of 15 and is playing, with a small frontal haematoma. He can go home once he has been back to a normal conscious state for at least an hour, is acting normally and is tolerating fluids.

explanation_correct: Monomorphic punched-out erosions and vesicles appearing in an area of active eczema, with fever and systemic upset, are typical of eczema herpeticum (disseminated HSV). The RCH Eczema guideline lists this as a complication needing prompt antiviral treatment (IV in severe cases), with consultation with the paediatric team. Periorbital involvement needs urgent ophthalmology review.

option_explanations.A: Impetigo causes honey-crusted lesions rather than monomorphic punched-out erosions.
option_explanations.C: Fever with punched-out erosions suggests infection.
option_explanations.D: Varicella lesions are widespread and at different stages, not clustered in eczematous skin.
option_explanations.E: This does not fit the picture.

key_learning_point: Punched-out erosions in eczematous skin with fever suggest eczema herpeticum, which needs prompt antiviral treatment.

subtopic: Clozapine review in primary care: actively ask about bowel habit
stem: A 39-year-old man with treatment-resistant schizophrenia has been stable on clozapine 400 mg daily for two years under shared care. He sees his GP in Logan, Qld, for a routine review. His blood monitoring is up to date and normal. He says he feels 'fine' and has no complaints.
lead_in: Which one of the following is the most important additional history to take at this visit?

options.A: Bowel habit, including stool frequency and any straining, pain or distension
options.C: Childhood developmental history

explanation_correct: Australian Prescriber notes that constipation affects 15–60% of people on clozapine at any time, is potentially life-threatening and should be treated and prevented aggressively. Clozapine-induced gastrointestinal hypomotility can progress to obstruction or ileus. Patients often do not volunteer symptoms, so bowel habit should be asked about at every review, and preventive aperients started at the first sign of constipation.

option_explanations.B: This does not change his monitoring.
option_explanations.C: This is not relevant to his current safety.
option_explanations.D: Caffeine can affect clozapine levels, but bowel habit matters more.
option_explanations.E: This is not a key clozapine adverse effect to screen for.

key_learning_point: Ask every patient on clozapine about bowel habit. Constipation is common and can be fatal.

subtopic: Recognising antidepressant withdrawal after abrupt cessation
stem: A 45-year-old woman in Bunbury, WA, stopped venlafaxine 225 mg daily abruptly four days ago after 3 years of treatment because she felt well. She now has dizziness, 'electric shock' sensations in her head when she moves her eyes, vivid dreams, irritability and tearfulness. She has no suicidal thoughts. Her symptoms began within 48 hours of stopping.
lead_in: Which one of the following is the most likely explanation?

options.A: Relapse of major depression
options.C: Vestibular neuritis

explanation_correct: The Australian Prescriber article on stopping antidepressants (2026) describes withdrawal symptoms that include physical symptoms (dizziness, sensitivity to light and sound, 'brain zaps' or electric shock sensations, vivid dreams, akathisia) and emotional symptoms (anxiety, irritability, low mood, tearfulness). Abrupt cessation, longer duration of therapy and certain drugs (venlafaxine, duloxetine, paroxetine) raise the risk. Her rapid onset after stopping, with brain zaps, points to withdrawal rather than relapse.

option_explanations.A: Relapse usually develops more gradually and does not cause brain zaps.
option_explanations.B: This occurs with excess serotonergic drug, not withdrawal.
option_explanations.C: This does not explain the emotional symptoms or the timing.
option_explanations.D: Her features are not those of elevated mood.

key_learning_point: Brain zaps, dizziness and mood symptoms soon after abruptly stopping venlafaxine suggest withdrawal.

subtopic: Tapering an SSRI in a low-risk patient
stem: A 30-year-old man in Canberra, ACT, has taken sertraline 100 mg daily for 9 months for a first episode of depression, which is now in full remission. After discussing it with his GP, he wants to stop. He has never had difficulty stopping a medication before.
lead_in: Which one of the following is the most appropriate plan?

options.A: Stop today
options.B: Taper over 12 months using 1 mg reductions
options.C: Switch to fluoxetine and stop in 2 days
options.D: Halve the dose every day for 4 days
options.E: Taper by 25–50% dose reductions over about 2–6 weeks, for example 100 mg to 50 mg to 25 mg and then stop

explanation_correct: Australian Prescriber (2026) states that in patients at low risk of withdrawal symptoms, guidelines recommend 25 to 50% dose reductions over 2 to 6 weeks, for example sertraline tapered at 2-weekly intervals from 100 mg to 50 mg, then 25 mg, then stopped. Patients at higher risk may need smaller reductions over months.

option_explanations.A: Stopping abruptly can cause withdrawal symptoms.
option_explanations.B: This is for higher-risk patients or those who have had difficulty stopping before.
option_explanations.C: This is not the recommended approach for a low-risk patient.
option_explanations.D: This is too fast.

key_learning_point: Low-risk antidepressant cessation: reduce by 25–50% over 2–6 weeks.

subtopic: Bipolar disorder in a woman of childbearing potential: avoid starting valproate
stem: A 26-year-old woman in Darwin, NT, has a new diagnosis of bipolar I disorder after a manic episode, which has been treated as an inpatient. She is not pregnant, is sexually active and may want children in future. The psychiatry registrar is choosing a long-term mood stabiliser and suggests sodium valproate because it worked quickly for her uncle.
lead_in: Which one of the following is the most appropriate response regarding valproate?

options.A: Valproate is the preferred first-line option for women of reproductive age
options.B: Valproate is acceptable if she takes folic acid 5 mg
options.C: Valproate is safe if stopped once pregnancy is confirmed
options.D: Valproate is only a concern for epilepsy, not bipolar disorder
options.E: Valproate should not be used unless other treatments are ineffective or not tolerated, because of its high teratogenic risk

explanation_correct: The Australian Epilim (sodium valproate) Product Information states that valproate should not be used in female children and women of childbearing potential unless other treatments are ineffective or not tolerated. This is because valproate has a high teratogenic potential, and children exposed in utero have a high risk of congenital malformations and neurodevelopmental disorders. Treatment must be started and supervised by a specialist. Other options should be used first.

option_explanations.A: The Product Information says the opposite.
option_explanations.B: Folic acid does not remove the risk.
option_explanations.C: Exposure in early pregnancy carries the risk.
option_explanations.D: The restriction applies across indications.

key_learning_point: Avoid valproate in women of childbearing potential unless other treatments are ineffective or not tolerated.

subtopic: Red flags of clozapine-induced gastrointestinal hypomotility
stem: A 48-year-old woman on clozapine 500 mg daily is brought to an emergency department in Shepparton, Vic. She has had three days of abdominal distension, colicky pain and vomiting, and today passed watery stools. Temperature 38.0 °C, pulse 118/min. Her abdomen is distended and tender, with absent bowel sounds. She also takes oxybutynin.
lead_in: Which one of the following is the most likely diagnosis?

options.A: Viral gastroenteritis
options.B: Clozapine-induced agranulocytosis with neutropenic enterocolitis as the first diagnosis
options.C: Neuroleptic malignant syndrome
options.E: Clozapine-induced gastrointestinal hypomotility with obstruction or ileus and overflow diarrhoea

explanation_correct: Australian Prescriber lists red flags of serious clozapine-induced constipation: abdominal pain, distension, vomiting, overflow diarrhoea, absent bowel sounds, and signs or symptoms of sepsis. Anticholinergic drugs such as oxybutynin add to the risk and should be avoided when possible. This needs urgent hospital assessment.

option_explanations.A: Absent bowel sounds and distension in a patient on clozapine point to hypomotility. The 'diarrhoea' is likely overflow.
option_explanations.B: Possible but less likely. The full blood count should still be checked.
option_explanations.C: There is no rigidity or altered mental state.
option_explanations.D: Fever and absent bowel sounds exclude this.

key_learning_point: Clozapine plus pain, distension, vomiting, overflow diarrhoea and absent bowel sounds suggests hypomotility or ileus, which is an emergency.

subtopic: Starting olanzapine: co-initiate metformin to limit weight gain
stem: A 22-year-old man with first-episode schizophrenia in Wollongong, NSW, is to start olanzapine after a shared decision with his psychiatrist. His BMI is 24 kg/m², and his fasting glucose and lipids are normal. He is worried about weight gain.
lead_in: Which one of the following is the most appropriate additional measure at the time of starting olanzapine?

options.A: Wait until he has gained 7% of body weight before acting
options.C: Add topiramate routinely
options.D: Start metformin at the same time, alongside lifestyle advice
options.E: No measures because his BMI is normal

explanation_correct: The RANZCP-endorsed INTEGRATE guidelines recommend lifestyle interventions for everyone and co-initiating metformin when starting antipsychotics with high metabolic risk, such as olanzapine or clozapine, to limit weight gain.

option_explanations.A: INTEGRATE recommends preventive co-initiation of metformin.
option_explanations.B: This is not the recommended agent.
option_explanations.C: This is not the first-line recommendation.
option_explanations.E: Weight gain with olanzapine is predictable.

key_learning_point: INTEGRATE: co-initiate metformin with olanzapine or clozapine.

subtopic: Prevalence from incidence and average duration (steady state)
stem: In a stable population in regional Victoria, the incidence of a chronic skin condition is 4 new cases per 1,000 person-years. The average duration of the condition is 5 years. Assume steady state and low prevalence.
lead_in: Which one of the following is the best estimate of the prevalence?
explanation_correct: At steady state with low prevalence, prevalence ≈ incidence × average duration = 4/1,000 per year × 5 years = 20 per 1,000 (2%).

option_explanations.A: This divides incidence by duration.
option_explanations.C: This is the incidence.
option_explanations.D: This adds the numbers.
option_explanations.E: This is an arithmetic error.

key_learning_point: Prevalence ≈ incidence × duration (steady state, rare disease).

subtopic: Incidence rate using person-time
stem: A cohort study in Adelaide follows 200 disease-free workers. 100 workers are followed for 4 years each and 100 for 2 years each (losses to follow-up). Over the study, 12 develop occupational asthma.
lead_in: Which one of the following is the incidence rate?

options.A: 60 per 1,000 people
options.C: 20 per 1,000 person-years

explanation_correct: Person-time = 100 × 4 + 100 × 2 = 600 person-years. Incidence rate = 12/600 = 0.02 per person-year = 20 per 1,000 person-years.

option_explanations.A: This is the cumulative proportion (12/200) and ignores person-time.
option_explanations.B: This uses 800 person-years.
option_explanations.D: This uses 400 person-years.
option_explanations.E: This misplaces the denominator.

key_learning_point: Incidence rate = new cases ÷ total person-time at risk.
reviewer_notes: Calculation item; no guideline dependency. Arithmetic checked by author 2026-10-07 (IST). Needs clinician sign-off.

subtopic: Herd immunity threshold from R0
stem: A public health unit in Queensland is modelling an outbreak of a vaccine-preventable infection with a basic reproduction number (R0) of 5. Assume homogeneous mixing and a vaccine that gives complete, lasting protection.
lead_in: Which one of the following is the minimum proportion of the population that must be immune to prevent sustained transmission?
explanation_correct: Herd immunity threshold = 1 − 1/R0 = 1 − 1/5 = 0.8, or 80%. If vaccine effectiveness is below 100%, the coverage needed is higher (threshold ÷ effectiveness).

option_explanations.B: This is 1/R0.
option_explanations.C: This is not derived from R0.
option_explanations.D: This is the threshold for a much higher R0, as with measles.
option_explanations.E: Herd immunity does not require full immunity.

key_learning_point: Herd immunity threshold = 1 − 1/R0.
reviewer_notes: Calculation item; no guideline dependency. Arithmetic checked by author 2026-10-07 (IST). Needs clinician sign-off.

subtopic: Ecological fallacy
stem: An analysis of Australian local government areas shows that areas with higher average household fluoride filter sales have higher rates of dental caries in children. A councillor concludes that children in households that buy fluoride filters are more likely to develop caries.
lead_in: Which one of the following best describes the main problem with this conclusion?

options.A: Recall bias
options.C: Ecological fallacy

explanation_correct: The data are aggregated at area level. Applying an association seen between groups to individuals is the ecological fallacy, because the children with caries may not be in the households that bought filters. Individual-level data are needed to support this inference.

option_explanations.A: No recall of past exposure is involved.
option_explanations.B: This applies to screening and survival.
option_explanations.D: This is a hospital-based selection bias.
option_explanations.E: This relates to occupational cohorts.

key_learning_point: Group-level associations cannot be assumed to hold for individuals (ecological fallacy).

subtopic: Bat exposure: test the bat and time PEP to the 48-hour result
stem: A 40-year-old man in Lismore, NSW, was scratched on the forearm this morning while removing a live microbat from his shed. He has never had rabies vaccine. He has captured the bat in a box, and the local public health unit says a lyssavirus result can be available within 24 hours. He has washed the wound well with soap and water.
lead_in: Which one of the following is the most appropriate next step?

options.A: Release the bat and start PEP
options.B: Arrange ABLV testing of the bat and withhold rabies vaccine and HRIG while the result is awaited
options.C: Start HRIG and vaccine immediately regardless of testing
options.D: No action because it was only a scratch

explanation_correct: The Australian Immunisation Handbook advises that, if possible, the bat should be kept and tested for Australian bat lyssavirus. After wound management, HRIG and rabies vaccine are withheld if the bat's ABLV status will be available within 48 hours of the exposure. If not, PEP starts as soon as possible. Bites to the head and neck are an exception: PEP is given promptly, preferably within 48 hours, even if the animal is being tested. If the bat tests negative, no PEP is needed.

option_explanations.A: Testing the bat avoids unnecessary PEP.
option_explanations.C: With a result due within 48 hours and a limb wound, PEP can be withheld.
option_explanations.D: Bat scratches are category II or III exposures.
option_explanations.E: Serology is not used to decide on PEP for an unvaccinated person.

key_learning_point: After a bat exposure, test the bat. If the result will be available within 48 hours (and there is no head or neck bite), PEP can wait.

subtopic: ABLV post-exposure prophylaxis in a non-immune immunocompetent person
stem: A 52-year-old wildlife carer in Townsville, Qld, was bitten through the skin on the hand by a flying fox two days ago. The bat escaped and cannot be tested. She has never had rabies vaccine and is immunocompetent. The wound has been washed.
lead_in: Which one of the following is the most appropriate post-exposure prophylaxis?

options.A: Rabies vaccine on days 0 and 3 only
options.B: No PEP because Australia is rabies-free
options.C: HRIG alone
options.E: HRIG infiltrated into and around the wound, plus rabies vaccine on days 0, 3, 7 and 14

explanation_correct: The Australian Immunisation Handbook bat-exposure algorithm states that a non-immune, immunocompetent person with a category II or III bat exposure should receive HRIG (if 7 days or less since the first vaccine dose) and 4 vaccine doses intramuscularly on days 0, 3, 7 and 14. HRIG is infiltrated in and around the wound as much as possible, with any remainder given intramuscularly away from the vaccine site.

option_explanations.A: This is the regimen for previously immunised people.
option_explanations.B: Australian bats can carry ABLV.
option_explanations.C: Vaccine is always needed.
option_explanations.D: This is the regimen for immunocompromised people.

key_learning_point: Non-immune, immunocompetent person with a bat bite: HRIG plus 4 vaccine doses (days 0, 3, 7, 14).
